name: Liam Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, Liam, and thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a blast-hole drill at a gold mine, open pit. The drill puts down holes about fifteen metres deep in a pattern, and then the shot crew fills them with explosive and blows the bench. I'm the lead on the drill crew, two rigs on days and two on nights. Most days I'm in the cab by seven, I check the bit and the compressor, and then I'm drilling to the pattern the engineers send. I like the feel of the rock through the controls. After thirty-four years you know hard ground from soft by the sound. What wears me out is the engineers changing the pattern three times a day from the office.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Has anything about the drilling changed lately?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: They had a demonstration of a driverless drill last year, a company brought it out to show the managers. It got stuck on soft ground by the second day and I had to tow it out with my rig. Everyone in the lunch hut still laughs about it, but I noticed the managers weren't laughing, they were taking notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, and leave it at that. I'm not one for going on about it online. I'd probably just mention it at lunch with the boys and get back to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I keep drilling until I'm sixty-five, which is what I want. I'm not sure the driverless drills are hype, though, AI or no AI. That one got stuck, but the next one might not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. I'd keep doing my job, keep my nose clean, and count down to the pension. Maybe I'd finally pay off the boat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. It's the way it should be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the boat.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a little aluminium fishing boat I bought five years ago, my one luxury, and I'm still paying it off. Nora says it's the reason we've got nothing in the bank, and she's half right. I go out on the dam every second Sunday, and that boat is the only place nobody sends me a new drill pattern.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools, or computers much at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I've got a phone for calls and the roster, and the grandkids show me the photos. I've never asked one of those chat things anything, and I don't plan to start.

S0.say: I told you so, and that's the end of it. He wouldn't post online, just mention it at lunch with the boys and get back to work.
S0.think: It means I keep drilling until sixty-five, which is what I want. But I'm not sure the driverless drills are hype, because the next one might not get stuck.
S0.do: Carries on exactly as now, keeping his head down and counting down to the pension. Hopes to finally pay off the fishing boat.
S0.feel: Fine; this is how things should be.
S0.quote: I go out on the dam every second Sunday, and that boat is the only place nobody sends me a new drill pattern.
S0.fieldNote: Liam is a quiet, private man who wants the next seven years to be like the last thirty-four. Even in the calm picture he admits the driverless drill could return. The fishing boat is his one luxury and also part of why he has no savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's just business, the way it's always been. Companies cut costs, and they'll do it with machines if machines are cheaper. I wouldn't make a song and dance about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me more than I'd let on. If a few years means three or four, I'm sixty-one or sixty-two when they bring the driverless rigs in properly. There's no other drilling job within two hundred kilometres.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job and hope they keep a couple of us on to watch the machines. I'd stop spending on anything that isn't needed, and I'd think about selling the boat. Mostly I'd wait and see what the company actually does before I do anything rash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It sits in my stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the company offered a course to supervise the driverless rigs, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say no, if I'm honest. I'm no good with screens, and I'd hate being the old fool in the classroom. Maybe if they made it part of the job, I'd go along, but I wouldn't volunteer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about it at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nora, but not straight away. I'd sit with it a week first. I don't bring the pit home. I'd tell Nora once I knew what I was going to do, not before.

S1.say: It's just business, the way it's always been: companies cut costs, and machines are cheaper. He wouldn't make a song and dance about it.
S1.think: It worries me more than I'd let on, because I'd be sixty-one or sixty-two when the driverless rigs come in. There's no other drilling job within two hundred kilometres.
S1.do: Keeps working and hopes a couple of operators are kept to watch the machines. Cuts unneeded spending, considers selling the boat, and waits to see what the company does before acting.
S1.feel: Anxious, a feeling that sits in his stomach.
S1.quote: I don't bring the pit home. I'd tell Nora once I knew what I was going to do, not before.
S1.fieldNote: Liam's public shrug of 'it's just business' covers real private worry about the gap before his pension. He wouldn't volunteer for supervisor training because he dreads looking foolish. He keeps things from his wife until he has a plan, which says a lot about him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say somebody has to do something, but I don't know who. Neither lot in government has a clue about places like ours. At work I'd say keep your heads down and see what the company offers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, it would finish me. Two years and I'm sixty, nothing saved, and the only skill I've got is the one the robot just took. I don't know what I'd do. I really don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell the boat straight away, and anything else worth anything, the second car, the tools I don't use. I'd ask the company what they'd pay out and take it if it covered the debts. Then I suppose I'd have to go and see the welfare people, which I've never done in my life, and lean on our daughter for a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked, truthfully. Like hitting a void in the hole and the drill dropping away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having only two years change what you'd try?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years there's nothing to try. A course takes a year, and then what, the robot does that job too. Two years isn't a warning. It's an eviction notice with the date filled in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lean on your daughter. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's got a spare room since her eldest moved out. Maybe we'd sell the house and move in with her, help with the grandkids. I'd hate it, being under her roof at my age. But I'd do it before I'd sit in the welfare office every week.

S2.say: Somebody has to do something, but neither side of government has a clue about places like ours. At work he'd tell the crew to keep their heads down and see what the company offers.
S2.think: It would finish me: two years and I'm sixty with nothing saved, and the only skill I have is the one the robot just took. I really don't know what I'd do.
S2.do: Sells the boat, the second car and spare tools straight away and takes any payout that covers his debts. Goes to the welfare office for the first time and leans on his daughter, possibly moving in with her.
S2.feel: Panicked, like the drill dropping into a void.
S2.quote: Two years isn't a warning. It's an eviction notice with the date filled in.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year picture leaves Liam out of options, and he said so without dressing it up. He blames no one specific, distrusting both sides of politics. Moving in with his daughter is a choice he would hate but prefers to regular visits to the welfare office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is something to work with. Keep your head down, save what you can, and don't believe everything you read. That's what I'd tell the young ones on my crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years and I'm sixty-three. Close, but not close enough. I'd be two years short of the pension, which on what I've got would mean the house or the boat or both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell the boat in the first year and put the money on the house. I'd do every overtime shift there is. I'd ask the payroll office the earliest I could retire with a reduced pension and work out if we could live on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but I can see the outline of what to do. That's better than the two-year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would five years change your mind about training to supervise the driverless rigs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. If it got me from sixty-three to sixty-five, I'd sit in a classroom and feel stupid for a while. I'd rather feel stupid in a classroom for two years than broke on a porch for twenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd sell the boat even with five years. Why so quickly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it'll be worth less every year, and every month I'm paying for it is a month I'm not paying for the house. It's the easiest thing to cut. I'd miss the dam, though.

S3.say: Five years is something to work with: keep your head down, save what you can, and don't believe everything you read. That's what he'd tell the young ones on his crew.
S3.think: Five years puts me at sixty-three, two years short of the pension. On what I've got, that gap means losing the house, the boat or both.
S3.do: Sells the boat in the first year and puts the money on the house, and works every overtime shift. Asks payroll about the earliest reduced pension and whether they could live on it.
S3.feel: Alarmed, but able to see the outline of a plan, which is better than with two years.
S3.quote: I'd rather feel stupid in a classroom for two years than broke on a porch for twenty.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Liam just enough room to plan, and he shifts on training if it bridges him to sixty-five. Selling the boat early is a clear-eyed choice that costs him his one escape. He is still losing sleep over the two-year gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and things never happen as fast as the experts say. At lunch I'd say I'll be fishing by then anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and I'm sixty-eight. I'd be retired, if they don't push me out first. So it's the one I can mostly ignore, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, much. I'd keep drilling, keep paying off the boat, and retire at sixty-five like I planned. If the company starts offering packages early, I'd look at them, but I wouldn't go chasing anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, mainly for the young guys on the crew. For me, not so much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marco, who's thirty and just bought a house. He's a good driller, but he'll be forty when it comes. I'll be on the dam with a line in the water, and Marco will be explaining to his kids why there's no drill for him to drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell Marco anything now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to learn the computer side, the stuff I won't do. He's young, he can pick it up. And to not buy a boat.

S4.say: Ten years is a long time, and things never happen as fast as the experts say. He'd tell the lunch table he'll be fishing by then anyway.
S4.think: By 2036 I'm sixty-eight and retired, if they don't push me out first. So it's the one I can mostly ignore.
S4.do: Carries on drilling, paying off the boat, and plans to retire at sixty-five. Would look at early packages if offered but chases nothing.
S4.feel: A bit uneasy, mostly for the younger men on his crew.
S4.quote: I'll be on the dam with a line in the water, and Marco will be explaining to his kids why there's no drill for him to drive.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Liam relaxes and turns his worry to younger crew like Marco. He'd tell Marco to learn the computer side he refuses to learn himself, a contradiction he seemed aware of. His joke about not buying a boat had real regret in it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, without question. Sixty, nothing saved, no other job out here. What would help is if they paid people my age through to the pension, just let us go early on a fair amount. I'm not after a handout, just what I'd have earned if they'd let me finish.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what we'd do with the time. I've drilled since I was twenty-four. I don't know who I am if I'm not the man on the drill.

headlineQuote: Everyone in the lunch hut still laughs about it, but I noticed the managers weren't laughing, they were taking notes.
portrait: Liam Reyes is a 58-year-old blast-hole drill lead at an open-pit gold mine, with thirty-four years on the rigs, a fishing boat he is still paying off and nothing in the bank. He is private, keeps his worries from his wife until he has a plan, and sees AI and automation as 'just business' rather than anyone's fault. He never uses AI and wouldn't volunteer for training, though five years' warning softens that if it bridges him to his pension. The two-year scenario leaves him panicked and out of options, while with ten years he expects to be fishing and worries instead for younger drillers like Marco.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he would be sixty with nothing saved and no other job nearby.
whatWouldHelp: Being paid through to his pension on a fair amount if pushed out early, which he sees as what he would have earned rather than a handout.
